# Paul Irving

## Overview

- **Age:** 16  <sub>[v3 c23 P6](../source/v03-c23.md#nw-v03-c23-p0006), [v3 c40 P2](../source/v03-c40.md#nw-v03-c40-p0002)</sub>
- **Gender:** Male  <sub>[v2 c5 P7](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0007), [v2 c11 P38](../source/v02-c11.md#nw-v02-c11-p0038)</sub>
- **Origin:** Avonlea  <sub>[v2 c1 P45](../source/v02-c01.md#nw-v02-c01-p0045), [v2 c5 P7](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0007), [v5 c3 P14](../source/v05-c03.md#nw-v05-c03-p0014)</sub>
- **Role:** Poet  <sub>[v4 c3 P33](../source/v04-c03.md#nw-v04-c03-p0033), [v5 c3 P14](../source/v05-c03.md#nw-v05-c03-p0014)</sub>

- **Nicknames:** Paul  <sub>[v2 c1 P45](../source/v02-c01.md#nw-v02-c01-p0045), [v2 c5 P7](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0007)</sub>

## Appearance

At ten years old, Paul was small for his age, with very dark blue eyes, a sensitive and delicate face, crimson lips, and chestnut curls. As he matured into his teenage years, he grew exceptionally tall, reaching six feet in height. By sixteen, his earlier curls were replaced with close-cropped brown locks, though he retained his beautiful face and eyes.

_Sources: [v2 c5 P7](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0007), [v2 c5 P8](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0008), [v2 c15 P1](../source/v02-c15.md#nw-v02-c15-p0001), [v2 c27 P24](../source/v02-c27.md#nw-v02-c27-p0024), [v3 c23 P6](../source/v03-c23.md#nw-v03-c23-p0006), [v3 c40 P2](../source/v03-c40.md#nw-v03-c40-p0002), [v4 c3 P30](../source/v04-c03.md#nw-v04-c03-p0030)_

## Personality

Paul possesses a deeply imaginative and artistic nature, often creating and speaking of imaginary 'dream-people' such as his rock friends on the shore. He is remarkably mature, thoughtful, and meditative, displaying grave manners that contrast with his youthful looks. Beneath his fanciful tendencies lies a manly, fair-minded character who stands up for himself and shows kindness to younger students. He is cleanly and polite, earning a reputation among adults as a perfect gentleman.

_Sources: [v2 c5 P8](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0008), [v2 c8 P32](../source/v02-c08.md#nw-v02-c08-p0032), [v2 c8 P52](../source/v02-c08.md#nw-v02-c08-p0052), [v2 c11 P38](../source/v02-c11.md#nw-v02-c11-p0038), [v2 c11 P42](../source/v02-c11.md#nw-v02-c11-p0042), [v2 c23 P36](../source/v02-c23.md#nw-v02-c23-p0036), [v2 c27 P5](../source/v02-c27.md#nw-v02-c27-p0005)_

## History

Paul Irving came from Boston to live with his grandmother on the shore road in Avonlea. Upon entering the local school, he instantly formed a bond with his teacher, Anne Shirley, who recognized his unique genius and poetic imagination. During his school days, he befriended Lavendar Lewis, sharing fanciful stories in her garden, and inadvertently helped reunite her with his father, Stephen Irving. Following his father's remarriage to Lavendar, Paul continued his education and grew into a tall young man interested in football as well as poetry. He wrote a lyric about a bird singing at Anne's wedding that was later published in his first volume of verse. He eventually moved back to the States, where his widely published poetry inspired Anne's son, Walter Blythe.

_Sources: [v2 c1 P45](../source/v02-c01.md#nw-v02-c01-p0045), [v2 c5 P7](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0007), [v2 c23 P36](../source/v02-c23.md#nw-v02-c23-p0036), [v2 c28 P21](../source/v02-c28.md#nw-v02-c28-p0021), [v2 c29 P1](../source/v02-c29.md#nw-v02-c29-p0001), [v3 c40 P2](../source/v03-c40.md#nw-v03-c40-p0002), [v4 c3 P30](../source/v04-c03.md#nw-v04-c03-p0030), [v4 c3 P33](../source/v04-c03.md#nw-v04-c03-p0033), [v4 c4 P16](../source/v04-c04.md#nw-v04-c04-p0016), [v5 c3 P14](../source/v05-c03.md#nw-v05-c03-p0014)_

## Background by volume

- Mother died three years prior to his arrival in Avonlea  <sub>[v2 c15 P4](../source/v02-c15.md#nw-v02-c15-p0004)</sub>
- Moved from the United States to live with his grandmother in Avonlea  <sub>[v2 c1 P45](../source/v02-c01.md#nw-v02-c01-p0045), [v2 c11 P38](../source/v02-c11.md#nw-v02-c11-p0038), [v2 c21 P83](../source/v02-c21.md#nw-v02-c21-p0083)</sub>
- Pupil of Anne Shirley at Avonlea school  <sub>[v2 c5 P7](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0007), [v2 c7 P7](../source/v02-c07.md#nw-v02-c07-p0007)</sub>
- Had published poems in magazines before his teacher's wedding  <sub>[v4 c3 P33](../source/v04-c03.md#nw-v04-c03-p0033)</sub>

## Quotes

> Please, teacher, I found these in Mr. Wright’s field, and I came back to give them to you because I thought you were the kind of lady that would like them, and because . . . I like you, teacher.  <sub>[v2 c5 P21](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0021)</sub>

> You see, teacher, it’s just three years today since my little mother died. It’s such a long, long time but it hurts just as much as ever . . . and I miss her just as much as ever. Sometimes it seems to me that I just can’t bear it, it hurts so.  <sub>[v2 c15 P4](../source/v02-c15.md#nw-v02-c15-p0004)</sub>

> Mrs. Lynde, father made a pretty good job of picking out my first mother and I could trust him to pick out just as good a one the second time.  <sub>[v2 c19 P22](../source/v02-c19.md#nw-v02-c19-p0022)</sub>

> I can’t do it, Grandma. I don’t really know if I can eat anything. I feel as if there was a dreadful lump in my throat.  <sub>[v2 c26 P35](../source/v02-c26.md#nw-v02-c26-p0035)</sub>

> You’ll never grow old, Teacher. You are one of the fortunate mortals who have found and drunk from the Fountain of Youth,—you and Mother Lavendar.  <sub>[v4 c3 P32](../source/v04-c03.md#nw-v04-c03-p0032)</sub>
